headline: Computer scientist Moritz Hardt says AI benchmark scores mean little on their own and proposes giving every model the same test preparation so that rankings can be trusted again.
score_reason: Thoughtful expert interview on a real problem in how AI models are judged; opinion and proposal, no new result.
importance_line: Benchmarks shape how companies, investors and buyers judge AI models, so flaws in them affect anyone choosing or funding AI systems, but this is one researcher's view in an interview and his fix is a proposal, not an adopted standard.
summary: Quanta Magazine interviewed Moritz Hardt, a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and author of the 2026 book The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks, who says the benchmarking system is broken because AI builders can prepare models for specific tests, so a score such as 90 percent says little about real ability. He argues that rankings of models have historically stayed stable across datasets and could be restored by giving every model the same benchmark-specific preparation, which he calls “altitude training.”
